Decentralized, Local-First Database Synchronization over Bluetooth Low Energy

Zero Internet. Zero Central Servers. Automatic Peer Reconciliation. Cryptographic Provenance.

docs.title: Welcome to AirDB
docs.text:
AirDB is an open-source, local-first database replication engine designed for off-grid operations. When mobile devices running AirDB enter Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) proximity (~10–30 meters), they automatically discover each other, negotiate causal state differences, and stream database mutations directly device-to-device.

Whether you are coordinating emergency disaster relief in camps without cellular towers, running pop-up POS cash registers at an outdoor festival, or syncing wildlife conservation logs in national parks, AirDB ensures your data stays synchronized without needing an internet connection.

docs.title: Acknowledgements & Prior Art
docs.text:
AirDB's protocols and architecture were informed by foundational research across distributed systems, local-first software, and wireless networking:

  • BitChat: For proving the viability of mobile Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) store-and-forward mesh communication. AirDB provides a clean-room implementation focused on structured database replication and causal consistency (CRDT/HLC) rather than ephemeral messaging.
  • Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC): Based on "Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases" by Sandeep Kulkarni, Murat Demirbas, David Madeppa, Bharath Balasubramanian, and Sugumar Radhakrishnan (2014).
  • Vector Clocks & Distributed Ordering: Grounded in the research of Leslie Lamport (1978), Colin Fidge (1988), and Friedemann Mattern (1988).
  • The Local-First Movement: Inspired by "Local-First Software: You Own Your Data, in spite of the Cloud" by Martin Kleppmann, Adam Wiggins, Peter van Hardenberg, and Mark McGranaghan (Ink & Switch, 2019).
  • SQLite Engine: Informed by D. Richard Hipp's architectural principles of crash resilience, Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), and zero-dependency embedded persistence.
  • Cryptographic RFC Standards: RFC 8439 (ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD), RFC 8032 (Ed25519 Signatures), and RFC 5869 (HKDF-SHA256).

docs.title: Introduction to AirDB
docs.text:
Welcome to the AirDB documentation!

AirDB is an open-source, local-first database synchronization engine designed to work completely off-grid. It allows mobile phones and embedded devices to sync database records directly with each other over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) without needing an internet connection, cellular coverage, Wi-Fi routers, or central cloud servers.

docs.title: The Problem AirDB Solves
docs.text:
Most modern software assumes an always-on internet connection. Applications save data to centralized cloud databases like Firebase, DynamoDB, or PostgreSQL. When you lose internet access, things break:

  • Disaster zones and emergency camps: Cell towers and power grids are frequently destroyed during earthquakes, floods, or hurricanes. First responders need to register survivors, track medical triage status, and manage emergency supplies immediately across dozens of handheld devices.
  • Off-grid commerce: Pop-up shops, night markets, and outdoor festival booths need multiple cashier tablets to share order queues, inventory counts, and payment tallies in crowded locations where mobile data networks are congested or unavailable.
  • Field operations and conservation: Wildlife rangers and field inspectors in national parks need to collect observation logs, GPS coordinates, and inspection checklists that automatically sync across patrol teams when they meet along the trail.

AirDB was built to solve these exact situations. When devices running AirDB come within Bluetooth range (around 10 to 30 meters), they automatically discover each other, negotiate what data is missing, and sync updates in seconds.

docs.title: Core Design Principles
docs.text: AirDB is built on three straightforward principles:

docs.title: 1. Local-First Means Local Writes Never Block
docs.text: Your application writes directly to its local database first. You never have to wait for a network response, spin a loading wheel, or worry about timeouts. The data is saved immediately to local disk using durable SQLite with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL). AirDB synchronizes those changes in the background whenever nearby peers appear.

docs.title: 2. Clean Separation (Sans-I/O)
docs.text: The engine separates business logic from hardware radios. The algorithms that calculate timestamps, resolve conflicts, and format binary packets do not contain any socket calls, Android Bluetooth delegates, or Apple CoreBluetooth objects. This makes the system extremely fast, stable, and testable: you can simulate a 10-node mesh network completely in memory in milliseconds without touching physical hardware.

docs.title: 3. Zero-Trust Security Across Untrusted Relays
docs.text: In a disaster area or public market, data often hops through intermediate phones before reaching its destination. AirDB protects your data on two levels: - Over-the-air encryption: Transmissions are scrambled using ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD so eavesdroppers cannot read or inject packets. - Author signatures: Every mutation is digitally signed by the original author with an Ed25519 private key. Even if an intermediate relay phone is running modified software, it cannot alter or forge your records without invalidating the signature.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: Before diving into code and tutorials, this page gives you a quick overview of what AirDB expects, the real-world characteristics of Bluetooth Low Energy, and the mental models that will help you design reliable off-grid applications.

docs.title: Who This Documentation Is For
docs.text:
AirDB is designed for: - Android Developers building apps in Kotlin with Jetpack Room, SQLite, or SQLDelight. - Apple Developers building apps for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, or watchOS using Swift, SwiftData, CoreData, or GRDB. - Distributed Systems Engineers looking for an off-grid replication protocol that guarantees convergence without relying on cloud coordination.

You do not need a background in advanced cryptography or distributed math to use AirDB. The high-level APIs handle packet serialization, encryption, and peer discovery out of the box.

docs.title: 1. Bluetooth Low Energy Is Not Wi-Fi
docs.text: BLE is designed for power efficiency, not raw file downloading: - Bandwidth: Effective throughput over BLE typically ranges from 20 KB/s to 80 KB/s, depending on physical distance, radio interference, and device chipset capabilities. - Packet Size (MTU): Raw BLE packets are small (typically between 23 and 512 bytes). AirDB automatically handles payload compression and splits larger packets into smaller chunks for you. - What to sync: AirDB is designed for structured data (such as survivor triage records, inventory changes, sensor logs, and JSON or Protobuf payloads). For large multi-megabyte photo or video attachments, the recommended pattern is to replicate the file metadata via AirDB, and trigger a direct high-speed transfer (such as Wi-Fi Aware or Wi-Fi Direct) only when needed.

docs.title: 2. Eventual Consistency & Last-Write-Wins (LWW)
docs.text: In an off-grid mesh, devices are separated by distance and time. Device A and Device B might both update the status of the same survivor while disconnected from each other: - AirDB tracks edits using Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC). Each edit receives an unambiguous timestamp that combines physical time, a counter, and a unique node identifier. - When Device A and Device B meet later, the update with the higher timestamp cleanly wins. - Deleted records are marked with tombstones so that older updates from stale devices cannot accidentally bring deleted rows back to life.

docs.title: 3. Your Database Stays Yours (BYOD)
docs.text: AirDB does not force you to rewrite your entire database layer. You can use our ready-to-go SQLite adapter, or write a thin wrapper around your existing Room, CoreData, or GRDB schema. AirDB only needs to know how to read new changes and apply incoming updates.

docs.title: Where to Get Help
docs.text: If you run into trouble while setting up AirDB or building your app: - Frequently Asked Questions: Check out our FAQ page for common operational questions. - GitHub Discussions & Issues: Report unexpected behavior or ask questions on our GitHub repository. - Architecture Decisions: If you are curious why a specific protocol design or cryptographic choice was made, read the Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).

docs.title: 1. What happens if a phone's battery dies and its clock resets to the year 1970?
docs.text:
AirDB uses Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) rather than relying on pure system wall-clock time.

When a phone with a reset clock connects to a nearby peer, its internal clock automatically ratchets forward to match the highest physical timestamp observed from that peer, plus advances a logical counter. All future local edits will be stamped newer than prior events, preserving correct ordering even without cellular time synchronization (NTP).

docs.title: 2. What happens if Node A deletes a record while an offline Node B edits it?
docs.text: AirDB tracks deletions using tombstones: - When you delete a record, AirDB stores a lightweight tombstone record with MutationType.DELETE and assigns it a timestamp. - If Node B reconnects later with an update that has an older timestamp than the tombstone, Node B's update is discarded, and the record remains deleted. - If a user explicitly edits the record after learning about the deletion, that new write will have a newer timestamp and the record will be recreated cleanly.

docs.title: 3. Does continuous Bluetooth Low Energy scanning drain the phone battery?
docs.text: AirDB is designed to be power-conscious: - Duty cycling: In production apps, background BLE scanning can be cycled (for example, active for 2 seconds, resting for 8 seconds) when devices are relatively stationary. - Compact advertising: Devices broadcast minimal 31-byte legacy packets (Service UUID and Node ID) to keep radio airtime low. - Payload compression: Packets larger than 256 bytes are automatically compressed using zlib Deflate, cutting transmission time and radio power by 50% to 70%.

docs.title: 4. Can I use AirDB to sync photos, audio recordings, or database backups?
docs.text:
Bluetooth Low Energy has a physical throughput ceiling around 20 KB/s to 80 KB/s.

AirDB is optimized for structured application data (such as survivor triage records, inventory tables, chat history, and JSON or Protobuf payloads). For large binary attachments (such as high-resolution photos or audio recordings): 1. Save the image to local storage and sync its file path, metadata, and SHA-256 hash across peers via AirDB. 2. When peers need the raw image file, trigger an out-of-band high-speed direct transfer (such as Wi-Fi Aware, Wi-Fi Direct, or Multipeer Connectivity).

docs.title: 5. Why use the built-in SQLite adapter instead of my existing Room or CoreData setup?
docs.text:
The built-in SQLite adapters (SqliteDbAdapter in :airdb-adapter-sqlite and SqliteDbAdapter in AirDbKit) are turnkey, zero-boilerplate engines that configure Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and indexed changelogs automatically.

However, if your application already uses Room, SQLDelight, GRDB, SwiftData, or CoreData, you do not have to switch. You can implement the AirDbAdapter interface on top of your existing tables in about 50 lines of code.

docs.title: 6. Can an intermediate phone modify or forge records when relaying data in a mesh?
docs.text: No. AirDB uses RFC 8032 Ed25519 digital signatures on every mutation record: - The device that creates the change signs the collection name, entity ID, mutation type, timestamp, and payload bytes with its private key. - Intermediate phones pass the signed record along unchanged. - Receiving devices verify the signature against the author's public key before saving changes. If a relay modifies a single byte of the payload or changes the timestamp, verification fails and the change is discarded immediately.

docs.title: 7. Does AirDbKit require external package dependencies on iOS or macOS?
docs.text:
No. AirDbKit has zero external SPM dependencies. It relies entirely on native Apple standard frameworks: - Cryptography: CryptoKit (ChaChaPoly, Curve25519.Signing, HKDF) - Persistence: libsqlite3 (built into the Apple operating system) - Compression: Apple Compression framework (zlib Deflate) - Radio Transport: CoreBluetooth

This means you will never encounter third-party dependency conflicts or supply-chain security alerts when embedding AirDbKit in your Apple apps.

docs.title: List of Features
docs.text: This page provides a comprehensive summary of all capabilities built into AirDB.

docs.title: 1. Local Persistence & Storage
docs.text:
• Built-in Durable SQLite Engine:
  • Out-of-the-box storage engine for Android/JVM (SqliteDbAdapter) and Apple platforms (SqliteDbAdapter in AirDbKit).
  • Automatically enables Write-Ahead Logging (PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL) and normal disk syncing (PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL) for concurrent, non-blocking reads and writes.
  • Automatically manages indexed changes in an append-only changelog table.
  • Pluggable BYOD (Bring Your Own Database) Seam:
  • Connect your existing application database via the simple AirDbAdapter interface.
  • Ready-to-use recipes for Android Jetpack Room, SQLDelight, Apple GRDB.swift, SwiftData, CoreData, and in-memory key-value maps.
  • Soft-Delete Tombstone Lifecycle:
  • Records deleted locally retain an authoritative tombstone timestamp.
  • Outdated mutations from disconnected devices are safely dropped, preventing deleted entities from resurrecting.

docs.title: 2. Distributed Synchronization & Causality
docs.text:
• Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC):
  • Generates strictly monotonic timestamps combining physical wall-clock time, an internal counter, and a node tie-breaker.
  • Tolerates device clock drift, dead batteries, and devices resetting to the year 1970 without corrupting ordering.
  • Vector Clock State Tracking:
  • Every device maintains a compact knowledge map of the latest timestamp seen from every peer.
  • When two devices meet, they compute the exact missing delta set in \(\mathcal{O}(|\Delta|)\) instead of transferring the entire database.
  • Deterministic Conflict Resolution (Last-Write-Wins):
  • When two users edit the same entity while separated, the change with the higher HLC timestamp wins deterministically across all nodes.
  • Guarantees eventual mathematical convergence without needing central consensus rounds.

docs.title: 3. Zero-Trust Cryptographic Mesh
docs.text:
• Cluster-Level AEAD Encryption (RFC 8439):
  • Protects data in transit using symmetric ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption with a 256-bit cluster key.
  • The entire binary packet header is bound into the authentication tag as Authenticated Additional Data (\(AAD\)), immediately rejecting tampered headers or spoofed sender IDs.
  • Generates a fresh 12-byte CSPRNG nonce for every transmitted packet.
  • Record-Level Digital Signatures (RFC 8032):
  • The original author digitally signs each mutation using an Ed25519 private key.
  • Prevents untrusted or compromised intermediate gossip relay phones from tampering with, forging, or backdating records.
  • Key Derivation (RFC 5869):
  • Derives operational cluster keys and session keys deterministically using HKDF-SHA256.

docs.title: 4. Bluetooth Networking & Framing
docs.text:
• Dual-Role BLE Concurrency:
  • Devices simultaneously operate as a GATT Central (scanning for peers) and a GATT Peripheral (advertising presence).
  • Single-Flight GATT Queue (GattOperationQueue):
  • Enforces strict one-at-a-time operation dispatching per link on Android.
  • Eliminates native Fluoride/BlueDroid driver packet drops and race conditions.
  • Swift Actor Concurrency:
  • On Apple platforms, AirDbKit runs the core engine inside a Swift actor for compile-time thread safety and non-blocking CoreBluetooth callbacks.
  • Automatic Payload Compression:
  • Payloads exceeding 256 bytes are automatically compressed with zlib Deflate, cutting transmission airtime and battery consumption by up to 70%.
  • MTU Fragmentation & Assembly Buffer:
  • Automatically slices packets larger than the link MTU into 13-byte fragment envelopes.
  • Reassembles chunks on the receiver with a sliding 30-second TTL to prevent memory leaks from abandoned connections.

docs.title: 5. Sans-I/O Simulation & Developer Experience
docs.text:
• Zero-Radio In-Memory Simulation:
  • Core synchronization logic is 100% decoupled from hardware sockets and OS drivers.
  • Simulate multi-node mesh networks with variable packet drop rates and delays directly in JVM unit tests in milliseconds.
  • Zero Third-Party Dependencies on Apple:
  • AirDbKit relies exclusively on Apple standard frameworks (CryptoKit, CoreBluetooth, Compression, and native libsqlite3).
  • Interactive CLI Demo:
  • Includes a runnable multi-node disaster relief simulation (:airdb-samples:airdb-sim-demo) demonstrating real-time offline edits, peer discovery, and convergence.

docs.title: Coding Standards & Engineering Discipline
docs.text: These engineering standards ensure that AirDB maintains high architectural integrity, stability, and readability across both Kotlin and Swift codebases.

docs.title: 1. Concurrency & Thread-Safety
docs.text:
1. State Isolation:
  2. Internal JVM collections shared across threads must use thread-safe data structures (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, or atomic primitives).
  3. Any mutable critical sections across multiple state fields must be guarded by locks.
  4. On Apple platforms, mutable engine state must be encapsulated within a Swift actor or protected by scoped locks (NSLock.withScopedLock).
  5. Non-Blocking Radio Callbacks:
  6. Never call Thread.sleep() or execute blocking disk I/O inside Bluetooth callbacks or event listeners.
  7. Use Kotlin Coroutines (CoroutineScope, launch, withContext) with appropriate dispatchers (Dispatchers.Default for CPU operations, Dispatchers.IO for disk adapters).
  8. In Swift, delegate methods must dispatch work asynchronously to actor tasks without stalling CoreBluetooth queues.

docs.title: 2. API Design & Clean Seams
docs.text:
1. Strict Sans-I/O Discipline:
  2. Core synchronization algorithms and wire codecs must never import Android Bluetooth classes (BluetoothGatt, BluetoothDevice) or Apple CoreBluetooth classes (CBPeripheral, CBCentralManager).
  3. All I/O must enter and leave through the universal AirDbTransport and AirDbAdapter interfaces.
  4. Platform Purity:
  5. airdb-core, airdb-protocol, airdb-crypto, and airdb-adapter-api must remain 100% pure Kotlin with zero dependencies on the Android SDK (android.*).
  6. AirDbKit must strictly rely on native Apple standard frameworks (CryptoKit, Compression, CoreBluetooth, and libsqlite3). Zero third-party SPM packages.

docs.title: 3. Cryptographic Invariants
docs.text:
1. Authenticated Wire Framing:
  2. Every encrypted packet must bind the complete wire header into the AEAD cipher as Authenticated Additional Data (\(AAD\)).
  3. Never decrypt payloads without verifying the Poly1305 MAC tag.
  4. Canonical Signing:
  5. Canonical signing buffers must deterministically serialize collection, ID, mutation type, HLC timestamp, and payload in Big-Endian order.
  6. Inbound records must be verified against author public keys prior to calling applyChanges.

docs.title: 4. Zero-Emoji Policy
docs.text: Strictly zero emojis across all code, tests, comments, docstrings, commit messages, PR descriptions, and documentation files.

docs.title: Contributing to AirDB
docs.text:
Thank you for your interest in contributing to AirDB!

AirDB is an open-source project designed to provide reliable, local-first database synchronization over Bluetooth Low Energy. We welcome bug reports, feature proposals, documentation improvements, and pull requests.

docs.title: 1. Zero-Emoji Policy
docs.text: This repository strictly enforces a Zero-Emoji Policy: - Do not use emoji characters anywhere: in source code, inline comments, docstrings, commit messages, PR descriptions, or documentation files. - Automated CI scanners will reject any commits or pull requests containing emoji characters. - Use clear headings, bullet points, and GitHub-style callouts ([!NOTE], [!TIP], [!WARNING]) for visual structure.

docs.title: 2. Commit Message Convention
docs.text:
AirDB follows the Conventional Commits v1.0.0 specification:

<type>(<scope>): <short summary in imperative mood>

[optional body explaining motivation and technical decisions]

[optional footer for issue references]

docs.title: Allowed Types
docs.text:
• feat: New user-facing feature or API capability.
  • fix: Bug fix or edge case resolution.
  • perf: Performance improvement (allocations, latency, throughput).
  • docs: Documentation updates.
  • test: Adding or correcting tests.
  • refactor: Code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature.
  • ci: CI/CD workflows and build automation.
  • chore: Tooling, version bumps, or dependency updates.

docs.title: Allowed Scopes
docs.text:
• core: State engine, HLC, Vector Clock, reconciliation.
  • protocol: Binary framing, codecs, compression, fragmentation.
  • adapter: Persistence seam, SQLite, Room, GRDB, SwiftData.
  • crypto: ChaCha20-Poly1305, Ed25519, HKDF.
  • ble-android: Android BLE transport and GattOperationQueue.
  • ble-apple: Apple AirDbKit and CoreBluetoothTransport.
  • sim: Virtual simulation network and transports.

docs.title: 3. Pull Request Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Keep Pull Requests Focused: A pull request should address a single bug fix or feature.
  2. Include Tests:
  3. For Kotlin modules: Add unit tests under src/test/kotlin.
  4. For AirDbKit: Add tests under AirDbKit/Tests.
  5. Verify Locally Before Submitting: 
    cd airdb
./gradlew test
    For Apple platforms: 
    cd airdb/AirDbKit
swift test
  6. Sign Off Your Work: Ensure all commits include your developer signature (git commit -s).

docs.title: Security Policy & Vulnerability Reporting
docs.text: AirDB takes security and data privacy seriously, especially because the engine is designed for disaster zones, emergency medical camps, and off-grid financial transactions.

docs.title: Supported Versions
docs.text: Version Supported 0.2.x Yes (Current release) < 0.2.0 No

docs.title: Reporting a Vulnerability
docs.text:
If you discover a security vulnerability in AirDB:

  1. Do not create a public GitHub Issue.
  2. Report the vulnerability privately via GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting.
  3. Include:
  4. A description of the vulnerability.
  5. Steps to reproduce or proof-of-concept code.
  6. An assessment of the potential impact (e.g. over-the-air packet injection, replay vulnerability, or unauthorized mutation).

We acknowledge receipt of security reports within 48 hours and provide regular status updates until a patch is released.

docs.title: ADR 0001: Sans-I/O Architecture for Core and Protocol
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Mobile peer-to-peer applications frequently suffer from high testing friction, queue deadlocks, and flakey integration tests when network sockets or Bluetooth hardware APIs are interwoven directly into business logic. BitChat's V3 rewrite specifically highlighted the maintenance overhead of callback closures bridging queues into state.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We decouple all state machines, causal clocks, data models, and binary protocol serializers completely from network and operating system I/O: 1. airdb-core, airdb-protocol, and airdb-adapter-api do not import any network or Android classes. 2. Inbound network data is ingested as raw byte arrays. 3. Outbound data is emitted as high-level packets or commands. 4. An in-memory virtual radio mesh simulator (airdb-transport-sim) is provided to test multi-node sync topologies without hardware.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive: 100% testable on pure JVM in milliseconds; 100% Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) ready.
  • Negative: Requires clean interface boundaries (AirDbTransport, AirDbAdapter) between modules.

docs.title: ADR 0002: Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) for Causality and Conflict Resolution
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: AirDB operates in partitioned, offline environments (disaster zones, outdoor markets) where devices have no access to NTP time servers. Device wall clocks can drift or be manually changed by users. Relying purely on physical timestamps leads to data loss or incorrect ordering.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
We implement a monotonic Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) that tracks both physical epoch milliseconds and an incrementing logical counter. Each HLC timestamp also appends the unique node ID as a deterministic tie-breaker: physicalTime - logicalCounter - nodeId

Conflicts on identical record keys are resolved using Last-Write-Wins (LWW) based on total HLC ordering: HlcTimestampA > HlcTimestampB

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive: Strict causality preservation, monotonic progression even across clock resets, deterministic convergence without consensus rounds.
  • Negative: Last-Write-Wins operates at the record level; fine-grained column-level conflict resolution requires field-level CRDTs in future iterations.

docs.title: ADR 0003: Single-Flight GATT Queue for Android BLE
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Android Bluetooth stack (BlueDroid/Fluoride) allows only one outstanding GATT operation per connection. Firing simultaneous writes from background coroutines causes silent packet loss or GATT error codes (e.g. status 133 or GATT_BUSY).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We introduce GattOperationQueue in airdb-transport-ble: 1. Every connection link owns a dedicated FIFO queue. 2. An inFlight state flag ensures that only the head operation is submitted to the OS. 3. The next operation is dispatched only when the driver invokes onCharacteristicWrite or onNotificationSent. 4. Transient errors are retried with exponential backoff before marking a link dead.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive: Complete elimination of race conditions and dropped packets on Android BLE.
  • Negative: Increases queuing latency slightly, bounded by BLE connection intervals (typically 7.5ms–15ms).

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: AirDB was initially demonstrated with an in-memory database adapter (MemoryDbAdapter). For production deployments in disaster triage and mobile POS systems, nodes require durable disk persistence that survives application termination, power loss, and battery depletion. Furthermore, Apple platforms require a lightweight storage engine without bringing in heavy third-party SPM or CocoaPods dependencies (such as Realm, CoreData overhead, or third-party wrappers).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We introduce durable SQLite storage adapters conforming to AirDbAdapter: 1. JVM & Android: SqliteAirDbAdapter in :airdb-adapter-sqlite. 2. Apple Platforms: SqliteDbAdapter in AirDbKit utilizing native libsqlite3 C-bindings. 3. Database Engine Configuration: - Write-Ahead Logging enabled via PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL. - Synchronous disk writes set to PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL. - Foreign keys enabled where applicable. 4. Change Tracking & Tombstones: - A dedicated _airdb_changes table records mutation types (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), HLC timestamps, author public keys, and signatures. - An index on hlc_timestamp ASC ensures range queries (getChangesSince) execute in \(\mathcal{O}(\log N + K)\) time. - Soft-delete tombstones prevent concurrent reconciliation from resurrecting deleted records.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive:
  • High write throughput and concurrent non-blocking reads via SQLite WAL.
  • Zero external package dependencies on Apple platforms.
  • Atomic transactions guarantee that delta batches are either applied in full or rolled back.
  • Negative:
  • Requires maintaining SQL schema evolution and tombstone compaction logic across two platforms.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: AirDB operates in ad-hoc, off-grid environments where nodes communicate via open Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) radio channels and multi-hop gossip topologies. This exposes data to three primary vulnerabilities: 1. Passive Eavesdropping: Third parties scanning 2.4 GHz RF channels can read plain-text survivor registries, medical notes, or commercial transactions. 2. Unauthorized Injection: Rogue devices within radio range can forge handshakes or inject corrupt database records. 3. Malicious Intermediate Relays: In a decentralized gossip mesh, intermediate devices forward packets. A compromised relay could alter record contents, swap IDs, or backdate HLC timestamps without detection.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We implement a two-layer Zero-Trust Cryptographic Mesh: 1. Cluster-Level Symmetric AEAD (RFC 8439 ChaCha20-Poly1305): - All packets between cluster members are encrypted with a 256-bit symmetric clusterKey. - Every packet generates a fresh 12-byte CSPRNG nonce. - The entire 23-byte (or 31-byte) wire header is passed as Authenticated Additional Data (\(AAD\)), binding version, packet type, flags, timestamp, and node IDs into the Poly1305 MAC tag. - Any packet with invalid MAC tag is discarded before parsing. 2. Record-Level Asymmetric Signatures (RFC 8032 Ed25519): - Each mutation is signed by its originating author using a private Ed25519 key. - The author's 32-byte public key and 64-byte signature are attached to the ChangeRecord. - The signature covers the canonical tuple: collection, id, mutationType, hlcTimestamp, and payload. - When enforceSignatures is active, receiving nodes verify the signature against the author public key. Compromised relays cannot tamper with records or timestamps without invalidating the cryptographic signature. 3. Key Derivation (RFC 5869 HKDF-SHA256): - Symmetric cluster keys and session materials are derived using HKDF-SHA256 with distinct domain separation tags. 4. Platform Native Implementations: - JVM & Android: Standard Java 17 JCA (ChaCha20-Poly1305 and Ed25519). - Apple Platforms: Pure native Apple CryptoKit (ChaChaPoly and Curve25519.Signing).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive:
  • Full confidentiality against over-the-air RF sniffing.
  • Authentic framing prevents spoofed packet injections.
  • End-to-end cryptographic provenance protects against compromised or untrusted intermediate mesh relays.
  • Zero external third-party dependencies on both JVM and Apple platforms.
  • Negative:
  • Over-the-air packet overhead: 12-byte nonce + 16-byte Poly1305 tag per encrypted frame.
  • Record overhead: 32-byte public key + 64-byte signature per signed mutation.
  • Increased CPU consumption for cryptographic signature verification during large initial sync batches.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Welcome! This section guides you through setting up AirDB in your project, creating your first local database, and synchronizing data between devices over Bluetooth.

docs.title: Recommended Learning Path
docs.text:
We recommend following these guides in order:

  1. Installation & Setup: Add AirDB to your Android Gradle or Apple Swift package configuration, and set up required Bluetooth permissions.
  2. 5-Minute Quickstart: Write your first working code to initialize the database, start the engine, and record a mutation.
  3. Apple Platforms Guide: Learn how AirDbKit leverages Swift concurrency and native Apple frameworks with zero third-party dependencies.
  4. Hands-On Tutorial: Walk through a complete, realistic scenario—building an offline disaster triage registry with two independent nodes.

docs.title: What You Will Need
docs.text:
• For Android Development: Android Studio, Kotlin 2.0+, and an Android device or emulator running Android 8.0 (API 26) or higher.
  • For Apple Development: Xcode 15+, Swift 5.9+, and a device running iOS 14+, macOS 12+, or watchOS 7+.
  • For JVM Simulation: Any desktop operating system with Java 17+ installed.

docs.title: Apple Platforms Guide (AirDbKit)
docs.text: AirDbKit is the native Swift implementation of the AirDB protocol, designed specifically for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and watchOS.

docs.title: Architectural Principles on Apple Platforms
docs.text: AirDbKit was engineered with three core principles:

docs.title: 1. Zero Third-Party Dependencies
docs.text:
AirDbKit does not require any third-party Swift packages or CocoaPods. It is built entirely on native Apple system frameworks: - Radio Networking: CoreBluetooth - Cryptography: CryptoKit (ChaChaPoly, Curve25519.Signing, HKDF) - Persistence: libsqlite3 (native C SQLite bindings included in every Apple OS) - Data Compression: Apple Compression framework (zlib Deflate)

This ensures zero supply-chain risk, zero version conflicts with other dependencies, and tiny binary overhead.

docs.title: 2. Swift Actor Concurrency Model
docs.text: The central engine AirDbEngine is implemented as a Swift actor: - Compile-Time Data Race Safety: All internal state (active sync sessions, vector clocks, and link queues) is isolated within the actor. - Asynchronous Delegates: Incoming CoreBluetooth events are dispatched into Swift tasks asynchronously without blocking Bluetooth radio threads.

docs.title: Installing AirDbKit
docs.text:
AirDbKit is distributed as a native Swift package:

  • Xcode GUI: Select File > Add Package Dependencies... and enter repository URL: https://github.com/untacorp/airdb.git (Dependency Rule: from 0.2.0).
  • Package.swift: 
    dependencies: [
    .package(url: "https://github.com/untacorp/airdb.git", from: "0.2.0")
]

docs.title: Basic Swift Integration
docs.text:
Here is a typical integration inside a SwiftUI or UIKit app:

import AirDbKit
import Foundation

@MainActor
final class SyncManager: ObservableObject {
    @Published var lastSyncedPeer: String = ""
    @Published var syncedChangeCount: Int = 0

    private var engine: AirDbEngine?
    private var adapter: SqliteDbAdapter?

    func startEngine() async throws {
        // 1. Locate documents directory for persistent SQLite database
        let docsDir = FileManager.default.urls(for: .documentDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
        let dbPath = docsDir.appendingPathComponent("posko_records.sqlite").path

        // 2. Open SQLite persistence
        let sqliteAdapter = try SqliteDbAdapter(databasePath: dbPath)
        self.adapter = sqliteAdapter

        // 3. Derive cluster encryption key
        let clusterKey = try HkdfSha256.deriveKey(
            secret: "disaster-relief-shared-secret".data(using: .utf8)!,
            salt: "airdb-v1".data(using: .utf8)!,
            info: "cluster-aead-key".data(using: .utf8)!
        )
        let authorKeyPair = try Ed25519Signer.generateKeyPair()

        // 4. Initialize CoreBluetooth transport
        let transport = CoreBluetoothTransport()

        // 5. Initialize AirDbEngine actor
        let airdb = AirDbEngine(
            nodeName: "field-team-ios-\(UUID().uuidString.prefix(4))",
            adapter: sqliteAdapter,
            transport: transport,
            clusterKey: clusterKey,
            authorKeyPair: authorKeyPair,
            enforceSignatures: true
        )

        // 6. Listen for incoming changes
        await airdb.addSyncListener { [weak self] peerId, count in
            Task { @MainActor in
                self?.lastSyncedPeer = peerId
                self?.syncedChangeCount += count
            }
        }

        // 7. Start radio operations
        await airdb.start()
        self.engine = airdb
    }

    func saveSurvivorRecord(id: String, name: String, triageStatus: String) async throws {
        guard let engine = engine else { return }

        let payloadJson = """
        {"name": "\(name)", "status": "\(triageStatus)"}
        """

        _ = try await engine.saveRecord(
            collection: "survivors",
            id: id,
            type: .insert,
            payload: payloadJson.data(using: .utf8)!
        )
    }
}

docs.title: Tutorial: Building an Off-Grid Disaster Triage App
docs.text:
In this step-by-step tutorial, you will build a realistic disaster response coordination system. We will create two independent nodes representing two remote emergency response posts:

  1. Posko Medis (Medical Triage Post): Treats injured survivors and logs medical supply requests.
  2. Posko Logistik (Logistics Camp): Manages food, blankets, and shelter supplies.

Both posts start completely separated with no internet or radio connectivity. Each post logs records locally. Then, volunteers move between camps, bringing their devices into Bluetooth range, and AirDB automatically reconciles both databases into complete synchronization.

docs.title: 1. Setting Up the Simulation Environment
docs.text:
To demonstrate this in an easy, repeatable way on your laptop without needing physical Android or iPhone hardware, we use AirDB's SimulatedNetwork and SimulatedTransport.

package io.airdb.tutorial

import io.airdb.adapter.MutationType
import io.airdb.adapter.sqlite.SqliteDbAdapter
import io.airdb.adapter.MemoryDbAdapter
import io.airdb.core.engine.AirDbEngine
import io.airdb.transport.sim.SimulatedNetwork
import io.airdb.transport.sim.SimulatedTransport
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking
import java.io.File
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit

fun main() = runBlocking {
    println("Starting Disaster Triage Synchronization Tutorial...")

    // Simulated radio space shared by both devices
    val network = SimulatedNetwork()

docs.title: 2. Initializing Posko Medis (Medical Post)
docs.text:
Posko Medis uses the durable SQLite adapter (SqliteDbAdapter) to store records on local disk:

    // 1. Initialize Posko Medis
    val dbFile = File("build/posko-medis.sqlite")
    if (dbFile.exists()) dbFile.delete()

    val dbMedis = SqliteDbAdapter.open(dbFile)
    val transportMedis = SimulatedTransport("posko-medis", network)
    val engineMedis = AirDbEngine("posko-medis", dbMedis, transportMedis)

docs.title: 3. Initializing Posko Logistik (Logistics Camp)
docs.text:
Posko Logistik uses an in-memory adapter (MemoryDbAdapter) to manage supplies and incoming evacuees:

    // 2. Initialize Posko Logistik
    val dbLogistik = MemoryDbAdapter()
    val transportLogistik = SimulatedTransport("posko-logistik", network)
    val engineLogistik = AirDbEngine("posko-logistik", dbLogistik, transportLogistik)

docs.title: 4. Seeding Offline Data While Disconnected
docs.text:
While both camps are disconnected, each team records local updates:

    println("\n[1] Posko Medis records survivor registrations offline...")
    engineMedis.saveRecord(
        collection = "survivors",
        id = "survivor-001",
        type = MutationType.INSERT,
        payload = """{"name": "Budi Santoso", "condition": "Stable", "bloodType": "O"}""".toByteArray()
    )
    engineMedis.saveRecord(
        collection = "medical_needs",
        id = "med-req-1",
        type = MutationType.INSERT,
        payload = """{"item": "Oxygen Tanks", "urgency": "High", "qty": 10}""".toByteArray()
    )

    println("[2] Posko Logistik records available emergency supplies offline...")
    engineLogistik.saveRecord(
        collection = "survivors",
        id = "survivor-002",
        type = MutationType.INSERT,
        payload = """{"name": "Siti Rahma", "condition": "Minor", "familyContact": "0812345678"}""".toByteArray()
    )
    engineLogistik.saveRecord(
        collection = "supplies_inventory",
        id = "supplies-01",
        type = MutationType.INSERT,
        payload = """{"item": "Ready-to-eat Meals", "qty": 1500}""".toByteArray()
    )

At this moment: - Posko Medis has 1 survivor (survivor-001) and 1 medical need. - Posko Logistik has 1 survivor (survivor-002) and 1 supply inventory record. - Neither camp knows about the other camp's data.

docs.title: 5. Volunteers Enter Bluetooth Proximity
docs.text:
A field volunteer walks from Posko Medis toward Posko Logistik. As their Bluetooth radios come within range (~10–30m), we start both engines:

    println("\n[3] Devices enter Bluetooth range...")
    val latchMedis = CountDownLatch(1)
    val latchLogistik = CountDownLatch(1)

    engineMedis.addSyncListener { peerId, changeCount ->
        println(" -> [Posko Medis] Reconciled and applied $changeCount mutations from $peerId")
        latchMedis.countDown()
    }

    engineLogistik.addSyncListener { peerId, changeCount ->
        println(" -> [Posko Logistik] Reconciled and applied $changeCount mutations from $peerId")
        latchLogistik.countDown()
    }

    // Start radio operations
    engineMedis.start()
    engineLogistik.start()

    // Wait for the 4-phase synchronization handshake to complete
    latchMedis.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    latchLogistik.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    delay(300)

docs.title: 6. Verifying Convergent State
docs.text:
Let's inspect the databases of both camps:

    val syncedSurvivorsAtMedis = dbMedis.getActiveRecords("survivors")
    val syncedSurvivorsAtLogistik = dbLogistik.getAllRecords("survivors")

    println("\n[4] State After Synchronization:")
    println("Posko Medis total survivors: ${syncedSurvivorsAtMedis.size}")
    syncedSurvivorsAtMedis.forEach { (id, record) ->
        println(" - [$id] -> ${String(record.payload)} (HLC: ${record.hlcTimestamp})")
    }

    println("\nPosko Logistik total survivors: ${syncedSurvivorsAtLogistik.size}")
    syncedSurvivorsAtLogistik.forEach { (id, record) ->
        println(" - [$id] -> ${String(record.payload)} (HLC: ${record.hlcTimestamp})")
    }
}

docs.title: Result:
docs.text: Both camps now hold 2 survivors (survivor-001 and survivor-002) with identical data and timestamps. The medical post also learned about available meals, and the logistics camp learned about the critical need for oxygen tanks!

dependencies {

    implementation("io.github.untacorp:airdb-core:0.2.0")

docs.title: 5-Minute Quickstart
docs.text: This quickstart shows you how to initialize a persistent SQLite database, start the AirDB synchronization engine, record a mutation, and listen for incoming updates from nearby peers.

docs.title: Step 1: Initialize Database & Cryptographic Keys
docs.text:
AirDB encrypts all transmissions with a cluster key and signs each record with an author key pair:

Kotlin (Android / JVM)Swift (Apple Platforms) 
import io.airdb.adapter.sqlite.SqliteDbAdapter
import io.airdb.core.engine.AirDbEngine
import io.airdb.crypto.Ed25519Signer
import io.airdb.crypto.HkdfSha256
import io.airdb.transport.ble.AndroidBleTransport
import java.io.File

// 1. Open a durable SQLite database file
val dbFile = File(context.filesDir, "airdb_triage.sqlite")
val adapter = SqliteDbAdapter.open(dbFile)

// 2. Derive a 256-bit cluster AEAD key from a pre-shared cluster passphrase
val clusterKey = HkdfSha256.deriveKey(
    ikm = "merapi-emergency-cluster-2026".toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8),
    salt = "airdb-salt-v1".toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8),
    info = "cluster-aead-key".toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)
)

// 3. Generate or load an Ed25519 signing key pair for this device
val authorKeyPair = Ed25519Signer.generateKeyPair()

import AirDbKit
import Foundation

// 1. Open a durable SQLite database file in the Documents directory
let docsUrl = FileManager.default.urls(for: .documentDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
let dbPath = docsUrl.appendingPathComponent("airdb_triage.sqlite").path
let adapter = try SqliteDbAdapter(databasePath: dbPath)

// 2. Derive a 256-bit cluster AEAD key from a pre-shared cluster passphrase
let clusterKey = try HkdfSha256.deriveKey(
    secret: "merapi-emergency-cluster-2026".data(using: .utf8)!,
    salt: "airdb-salt-v1".data(using: .utf8)!,
    info: "cluster-aead-key".data(using: .utf8)!
)

// 3. Generate or load an Ed25519 signing key pair for this device
let authorKeyPair = try Ed25519Signer.generateKeyPair()

docs.title: Step 2: Initialize & Start AirDbEngine
docs.text:
Connect the persistence adapter and the radio transport to create the central coordinating engine:

Kotlin (Android / JVM)Swift (Apple Platforms) 
// 4. Create the BLE transport and start the engine
val transport = AndroidBleTransport(context)
val engine = AirDbEngine(
    nodeName = "posko-merapi-1",
    adapter = adapter,
    transport = transport,
    clusterKey = clusterKey,
    authorKeyPair = authorKeyPair,
    enforceSignatures = true
)

// 5. Register a listener to receive notifications when changes arrive from peers
engine.addSyncListener { peerId, changeCount ->
    println("Synchronized $changeCount verified changes from peer: $peerId")
}

// 6. Start Bluetooth advertising and scanning
engine.start()

// 4. Create the CoreBluetooth transport and initialize the actor engine
let transport = CoreBluetoothTransport()
let engine = AirDbEngine(
    nodeName: "posko-merapi-ios-1",
    adapter: adapter,
    transport = transport,
    clusterKey: clusterKey,
    authorKeyPair: authorKeyPair,
    enforceSignatures: true
)

// 5. Register a listener for synchronization progress
await engine.addSyncListener { peerId, changeCount in
    print("Synchronized \(changeCount) verified changes from peer: \(peerId)")
}

// 6. Start Bluetooth radio operations
await engine.start()

docs.title: Step 3: Record a Local Mutation
docs.text:
When you write data locally, use engine.saveRecord. The engine assigns it an authoritative Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) timestamp, signs it with your device's private key, writes it to the local SQLite database, and streams the change immediately to any connected peers:

Kotlin (Android / JVM)Swift (Apple Platforms) 
import io.airdb.adapter.MutationType
import kotlinx.coroutines.launch
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking

val survivorJson = """{"name": "Budi Santoso", "status": "Treated", "triage": "GREEN"}"""

// Save record to the "survivors" collection
val changeRecord = engine.saveRecord(
    collection = "survivors",
    id = "survivor-101",
    type = MutationType.INSERT,
    payload = survivorJson.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)
)

println("Saved record with HLC timestamp: ${changeRecord.hlcTimestamp}")

let survivorJson = """{"name": "Budi Santoso", "status": "Treated", "triage": "GREEN"}"""
let payload = survivorJson.data(using: .utf8)!

// Save record to the "survivors" collection
let changeRecord = try await engine.saveRecord(
    collection: "survivors",
    id: "survivor-101",
    type: .insert,
    payload: payload
)

print("Saved record with HLC timestamp: \(changeRecord.hlcTimestamp)")

docs.title: What Happens Next?
docs.text:
1. When another device running AirDB with the same cluster key comes within Bluetooth range, both phones detect each other.
  2. They perform a 4-phase synchronization handshake.
  3. They compare what they have seen using vector clocks, and stream only the missing records.
  4. The listener callback fires with the number of verified records applied!

Continue to the Hands-On Tutorial for a deeper look at building an offline disaster triage app with multi-node replication.

docs.title: How Synchronization Works
docs.text: This chapter explains how AirDB tracks changes across disconnected devices, decides who edited what, and guarantees that every device converges to identical data without a central server.

docs.title: 1. Why Physical Clocks Aren't Enough
docs.text:
In normal web development, the backend server assigns timestamps: created_at = NOW().

In an off-grid disaster area or remote field camp, there is no central server. Devices rely on their internal battery clocks. However: - A phone battery might die, resetting the clock to January 1, 1970. - Two phones might differ by 3 minutes due to crystal oscillator drift. - If we simply trusted each phone's physical clock, an edit made yesterday on a device with a fast clock could accidentally overwrite a true newer edit made today.

To solve this, AirDB uses Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).

docs.title: 2. Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)
docs.text:
An HLC timestamp consists of three parts:

Timestamp = (physical_time, logical_counter, node_id)
  1. physical_time: The device's current wall-clock time in milliseconds.
  2. logical_counter: An incrementing counter (0, 1, 2...) for multiple edits that occur within the exact same millisecond.
  3. node_id: A unique device name or ID used as a tie-breaker if two devices create an edit at the exact same physical millisecond and counter.

docs.title: How Timestamps Progress
docs.text:
• Local Writes: When you save a record locally, your clock sets physical_time = max(last_known_time, now()). If now() hasn't advanced, it increments logical_counter.
  • Learning from Peers: When you receive an update from a nearby peer with a higher timestamp, your clock immediately ratchets forward to match the peer's time. Your clock will never step backward, even if your phone's battery died.

docs.title: Comparing Two Timestamps
docs.text:
Comparing two HLC timestamps is simple and deterministic: 1. Compare physical_time. Whichever is larger wins. 2. If physical_time is tied, compare logical_counter. Whichever is larger wins. 3. If both are tied, compare node_id alphabetically as a deterministic tie-breaker.

Because of this total ordering, every device in the mesh reaches the exact same conclusion about which edit came last.

docs.title: 3. Vector Clocks: Knowing What You Missed
docs.text:
When two phones connect over Bluetooth, we do not want to re-send the entire database over slow radio bandwidth. We only want to transmit what the other device hasn't seen yet.

AirDB tracks this with a Vector Clock: a lightweight dictionary mapping each known device name to the latest HLC timestamp seen from that device:

{
  "posko-medis": "1710928300000-0-posko-medis",
  "posko-logistik": "1710928295000-2-posko-logistik"
}

When Phone A meets Phone B: 1. Phone B sends its knowledge map: "Here is the newest timestamp I have seen from each device." 2. Phone A compares its own changelog against Phone B's map. 3. Phone A only sends records that have timestamps newer than what Phone B has seen. 4. Bandwidth is kept minimal: \(\mathcal{O}(|\text{new changes}|)\) instead of \(\mathcal{O}(|\text{entire database}|)\).

docs.title: 4. The 4-Phase Synchronization Handshake
docs.text:
When two devices connect over Bluetooth Low Energy, they execute a 4-step conversation:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Device A (Scanner / Central)
    participant B as Device B (Advertiser / Peripheral)

    Note over A,B: Phase 1 & 2: Identity & Cluster Authentication
    A->>B: Phase 1: HANDSHAKE (NodeID, Protocol Version)
    B-->>A: Phase 2: HANDSHAKE_ACK (Cluster Verified, Session OK)

    Note over A,B: Phase 3: Reconciliation & Delta Streaming
    A->>B: Phase 3a: RECONCILE_REQ (Vector Clock A)
    B-->>A: Phase 3b: RECONCILE_RESP (Vector Clock B)
    B->>A: Phase 3c: DELTA_BATCH (Missing changes B -> A)
    A->>B: Phase 3d: DELTA_BATCH (Missing changes A -> B)

    Note over A,B: Phase 4: Acknowledgment & Convergence
    A-->>B: Phase 4: DELTA_ACK (Confirm batch applied)
    B-->>A: Phase 4: DELTA_ACK (Confirm batch applied)

    Note over A,B: State: SYNCHRONIZED (Live Mutations Stream in Real-Time)

docs.text:
Because AirDB exchanges compact vector clocks rather than dumping full table snapshots, state reconciliation scales predictably with network diameter:

    x-axis ["2 Peers", "5 Peers", "10 Peers", "20 Peers", "50 Peers"]

docs.title: Real-Time Updates
docs.text: Once the initial 4-phase synchronization is complete, both devices stay in the SYNCHRONIZED state. If a user saves a new record while connected, AirDB streams that single mutation across the active link immediately without repeating the full handshake.

docs.title: Last-Write-Wins (LWW)
docs.text: If Nurse Siti updates survivor #101 on Phone A, and Doctor Budi updates survivor #101 on Phone B while disconnected: - Both updates are stored locally with their respective HLC timestamps. - When Phone A and Phone B connect, the record with the newer HLC timestamp wins and overwrites the older version.

docs.title: Deletions with Tombstones
docs.text:
If we simply erased a row from SQLite when a user clicked "Delete", an offline phone that hasn't heard about the deletion would send its copy back during the next sync, accidentally resurrecting the record!

To prevent this: 1. Deleting an entity creates a tombstone record with MutationType.DELETE and an HLC timestamp. 2. When an old update arrives from a peer with an older timestamp than the tombstone, AirDB rejects it. 3. If a user intentionally creates a new record with the same ID after the deletion, it receives a newer timestamp and is recreated cleanly.

docs.title: 6. The Convergence Guarantee
docs.text:
Because every node uses identical HLC comparison rules and deterministic Last-Write-Wins, distributed systems theory guarantees Strong Eventual Consistency:

As long as devices occasionally come within Bluetooth range of one another (directly or through intermediate gossip hops), every replica will converge to 100% identical state without needing a central coordinator.

docs.title: Security & Zero-Trust Cryptographic Mesh
docs.text:
In a distributed mesh network, data doesn't just travel point-to-point. Packets often bounce across intermediate volunteer phones before reaching their final destination.

In emergency response camps or outdoor markets, those intermediate devices might be untrusted, running modified software, or accidentally misconfigured. AirDB uses a Zero-Trust Cryptographic Mesh to ensure that data remains private and impossible to tamper with.

flowchart TD
    L1["Layer 1: Cluster-Level AEAD Encryption (ChaCha20-Poly1305)<br/>Scrambles over-the-air packets; binds headers so outsiders cannot inject data."]
    L2["Layer 2: Record-Level Digital Signatures (Ed25519)<br/>Proves who wrote each change; prevents intermediate relay phones from tampering."]
    L3["Layer 3: Key Derivation & Session Materials (HKDF-SHA256)<br/>Deterministically derives cluster and session keys from a single passphrase."]

    L1 --> L2
    L2 --> L3

docs.title: Layer 1: Over-the-Air Cluster Encryption (ChaCha20-Poly1305)
docs.text:
When devices communicate over Bluetooth Low Energy, anyone nearby with a radio packet sniffer could potentially listen in.

AirDB uses RFC 8439 ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) with a 256-bit cluster key:

  1. Confidentiality: All payload bytes (names, medical records, sales data) are encrypted on the wire.
  2. Fresh Nonce per Packet: A fresh, random 12-byte CSPRNG nonce is generated for every transmission to prevent replay attacks.
  3. Header Authentication Binding (AAD): The entire packet header—including the sender ID, timestamp, and packet type—is passed as Authenticated Additional Data (\(AAD\)) into the Poly1305 authenticator.

[!NOTE] If an attacker tampers with the sender ID or flips a single bit in the header, the Poly1305 MAC check immediately fails. AirDB drops the corrupted packet before attempting to parse it.

docs.title: Layer 2: Record-Level Digital Signatures (Ed25519)
docs.text:
Cluster encryption protects data between immediate radio peers. But what happens in a multi-hop mesh where Device A hands a packet to volunteer Device B to deliver to headquarters Device C?

Device B decrypts the radio packet to inspect where it should be routed. If Device B is malicious, could it alter a survivor's name or fake a medicine inventory count?

No. AirDB stops this with RFC 8032 Ed25519 digital signatures:

  1. Canonical Signing: When Doctor Budi saves a record on Phone A, Phone A bundles: 
    DataToSign = collection + id + mutation_type + hlc_timestamp + payload
  2. Author Signature: Phone A signs this data using its private Ed25519 key, attaching its 32-byte public key and 64-byte signature to the record.
  3. Relay Verification: When Headquarters Phone C receives the record, it checks the digital signature against Doctor Budi's public key.

If an intermediate phone altered the payload, modified the timestamp, or faked an edit, the cryptographic math fails and Phone C rejects the mutation immediately. The fake record is never written to disk or shared further.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Phone A (Author / Dr. Budi)
    participant B as Phone B (Untrusted Intermediate Relay)
    participant C as Phone C (Headquarters)

    Note over A: 1. Author signs mutation:<br/>Sign(Payload + HLC, Ed25519 Private Key)
    A->>B: 2. Transmit Encrypted Radio Packet (Cluster Key)
    Note over B: 3. Intermediate phone decrypts packet.<br/>Tampering with payload invalidates author signature!
    B->>C: 4. Relay packet over next BLE hop
    Note over C: 5. Verify Ed25519 Signature against Dr. Budi's Public Key.<br/>Tampered packet is immediately rejected and dropped.

docs.title: Layer 3: Key Derivation (HKDF-SHA256)
docs.text:
Rather than managing complex raw 32-byte hexadecimal keys, teams can share a human-readable cluster passphrase. AirDB uses RFC 5869 HKDF-SHA256 to derive cryptographically secure keys:

KotlinSwift 
import io.airdb.crypto.HkdfSha256

val clusterKey = HkdfSha256.deriveKey(
    ikm = "merapi-relief-camp-2026".toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8),
    salt = "airdb-v1".toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8),
    info = "cluster-aead-key".toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)
)

import AirDbKit

let clusterKey = try HkdfSha256.deriveKey(
    secret: "merapi-relief-camp-2026".data(using: .utf8)!,
    salt: "airdb-v1".data(using: .utf8)!,
    info: "cluster-aead-key".data(using: .utf8)!
)

docs.title: Networking, Framing & BLE Transports
docs.text: This chapter covers how AirDB packages data into binary frames, compresses large messages, splits packets across small Bluetooth Low Energy MTU limits, and manages hardware radios reliably.

docs.title: Key Header Fields
docs.text:
• Magic (0x41 0x44): Fixed bytes representing ASCII "AD" for AirDB. Rejects stray packets from unrelated Bluetooth accessories or devices.
  • Type (1 byte): Indicates the message purpose (HANDSHAKE, RECONCILE_REQ, DELTA_BATCH, DELTA_ACK, etc.).
  • Flags (1 byte):
  • 0x01 (FLAG_COMPRESSED): Set if the payload was compressed with zlib Deflate.
  • 0x02 (FLAG_HAS_RECIPIENT): Set if an optional 8-byte recipient ID is included in the header.
  • 0x04 (FLAG_ENCRYPTED): Set if the payload is encrypted with ChaCha20-Poly1305.
  • Payload Length (2 bytes): Exact length of the payload in Big-Endian network byte order.

docs.title: 2. Automated Payload Compression
docs.text:
Bluetooth Low Energy radio airtime directly impacts device battery life.

When a serialized payload exceeds 256 bytes, AirDB automatically compresses it using zlib Deflate before transmission. On typical JSON records and delta batches, this achieves a 50% to 70% size reduction, cutting radio transmission time and energy consumption significantly.

xychart-beta
    title "Payload Size: Raw JSON vs zlib Deflate (Bytes)"
    x-axis ["256B", "512B", "1024B", "2048B", "4096B"]
    y-axis "Wire Bytes" 0 --> 4200
    bar [256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096]
    line [256, 218, 384, 692, 1280]

If a payload is smaller than 256 bytes, AirDB leaves it uncompressed to avoid compression overhead.

docs.title: 3. MTU Fragmentation & Reassembly
docs.text:
Standard Bluetooth Low Energy connections have a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) that is often bounded (typically between 180 and 512 bytes). If a batch of mutations is 2,000 bytes, sending it all at once causes the Bluetooth driver to drop it.

xychart-beta
    title "Effective BLE Throughput by Link MTU Size (KB/s)"
    x-axis ["MTU 23 (Legacy)", "MTU 185", "MTU 247", "MTU 512 (Modern)"]
    y-axis "Throughput (KB/s)" 0 --> 30
    bar [1.8, 8.4, 14.2, 24.6]

AirDB includes an automated chunking system: 1. If a packet exceeds the link's safe MTU threshold (default 460 bytes), it is sliced into fragments. 2. Each slice is wrapped in a 13-byte FragmentHeader: 

+--------------------+------------------+------------------+--------------------+------------+
| Fragment ID (8B)   | Index (2B BE)    | Total (2B BE)    | Original Type (1B) | Chunk Data |
+--------------------+------------------+------------------+--------------------+------------+
3. The receiving device buffers incoming chunks in an AssemblyBuffer. 4. Once all chunks arrive, they are assembled back into the original AirDbPacket and processed.

[!TIP] Sliding 30-Second TTL: The AssemblyBuffer automatically purges incomplete fragment sets after 30 seconds. If a user walks away mid-transfer and connection drops, stale chunks will never leak device memory.

docs.title: 4. Concurrency: Solving the Android Bluetooth Queue Bug
docs.text:
A known issue in Android's native Bluetooth stack (Fluoride/BlueDroid) is that GATT operations are strictly asynchronous and single-flight per connection.

If an application invokes writeCharacteristic while another write is still pending in the hardware stack, Android either drops the packet silently or throws an immediate GATT_FAILURE error.

AirDB solves this on Android with the GattOperationQueue: - Every physical Bluetooth link maintains an isolated FIFO queue. - When an operation is queued, it is only dispatched to the Android Bluetooth driver when the previous operation triggers the hardware confirmation callback (onCharacteristicWrite or onNotificationSent). - If a transient radio error occurs, the queue automatically retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff before reporting a link failure.

On Apple platforms, AirDbKit runs the core engine inside a Swift actor, guaranteeing thread safety and asynchronous dispatch across CoreBluetooth delegate queues.

docs.title: 5. Dual-Role Radio Operation
docs.text:
In AirDB, devices do not act solely as clients or servers. Every device operates simultaneously in dual roles: - GATT Central: Scans for advertisements from nearby peers. - GATT Peripheral: Broadcasts its presence using a compact 31-byte advertising frame containing AirDB's 128-bit Service UUID.

This symmetric discovery ensures that any two phones approaching each other in the field can immediately establish a connection without requiring manual pairing or designated master nodes.

docs.title: Bring Your Own Database (BYOD)
docs.text:
AirDB is database-agnostic. While it includes turnkey, production-grade SQLite engines for Android and Apple platforms, it does not force you to replace your application's existing database architecture.

Instead, AirDB interacts with local storage through a clean interface: AirDbAdapter.

docs.title: The AirDbAdapter Interface
docs.text:
Any database—whether Room, SQLDelight, GRDB, CoreData, Realm, or a custom key-value store—can participate in AirDB replication by implementing four simple methods:

KotlinSwift 
package io.airdb.adapter

interface AirDbAdapter {
    // 1. Return records with HLC timestamp strictly newer than sinceHlcTimestamp
    suspend fun getChangesSince(sinceHlcTimestamp: String?, limit: Int = 100): List<ChangeRecord>

    // 2. Apply incoming remote mutations to the local database
    suspend fun applyChanges(changes: List<ChangeRecord>)

    // 3. Return the highest HLC timestamp currently stored locally
    suspend fun getLatestHlc(): String?

    // 4. (Optional) Filter changes missing on a peer given its vector clock
    suspend fun getMissingChanges(peerClock: Map<String, String>, limit: Int = 500): List<ChangeRecord>
}

import Foundation

public protocol AirDbAdapter: Sendable {
    // 1. Return records with HLC timestamp strictly newer than sinceHlcTimestamp
    func getChangesSince(sinceHlcTimestamp: String?, limit: Int) async throws -> [ChangeRecord]

    // 2. Apply incoming remote mutations to the local database
    func applyChanges(_ changes: [ChangeRecord]) async throws

    // 3. Return the highest HLC timestamp currently stored locally
    func getLatestHlc() async throws -> String?

    // 4. (Optional) Filter changes missing on a peer given its vector clock
    func getMissingChanges(peerClock: [String: String], limit: Int) async throws -> [ChangeRecord]
}

docs.title: Core Invariants for Custom Adapters
docs.text: When building a custom adapter for your database, keep these three rules in mind:

docs.title: 1. Idempotency & Last-Write-Wins (LWW)
docs.text: In distributed systems, the same mutation may be received multiple times across different gossip hops. Your applyChanges implementation MUST be idempotent: - If an incoming record has an older or identical HLC timestamp compared to what is already stored locally for that entity ID, ignore it. - If the incoming record has a newer HLC timestamp, overwrite the local record.

docs.title: 2. Append-Only Changelog or Index
docs.text: To respond quickly to getChangesSince, maintain an index or a dedicated changelog table where entries are ordered by HLC timestamp ascending.

docs.title: 3. Tombstones for Deletions
docs.text: Never execute an immediate DELETE FROM table WHERE id = ? without recording a tombstone: - Store a tombstone entry with MutationType.DELETE and the deletion's HLC timestamp. - If an outdated node attempts to sync an older version of that entity later, the tombstone prevents the deleted record from reappearing.

docs.title: 2. Implementing AirDbAdapter
docs.text:
import AirDbKit
import CoreData
import Foundation

public final class CoreDataAirDbAdapter: AirDbAdapter, @unchecked Sendable {
    private let persistentContainer: NSPersistentContainer

    public init(persistentContainer: NSPersistentContainer) {
        self.persistentContainer = persistentContainer
    }

    public func getChangesSince(sinceHlcTimestamp: String?, limit: Int) async throws -> [ChangeRecord] {
        try await persistentContainer.performBackgroundTask { context in
            let request = NSFetchRequest<NSManagedObject>(entityName: "AirDbChangeEntity")

            if let since = sinceHlcTimestamp {
                request.predicate = NSPredicate(format: "hlcTimestamp > %@", since)
            }
            request.sortDescriptors = [NSSortDescriptor(key: "hlcTimestamp", ascending: true)]
            request.fetchLimit = limit

            let results = try context.fetch(request)
            return results.compactMap { obj -> ChangeRecord? in
                guard let id = obj.value(forKey: "recordId") as? String,
                      let collection = obj.value(forKey: "collection") as? String,
                      let rawType = obj.value(forKey: "mutationType") as? Int16,
                      let type = MutationType(rawValue: Int(rawType)),
                      let hlc = obj.value(forKey: "hlcTimestamp") as? String else {
                    return nil
                }

                let payload = obj.value(forKey: "payload") as? Data ?? Data()
                let authorPublicKey = obj.value(forKey: "authorPublicKey") as? Data
                let signature = obj.value(forKey: "signature") as? Data

                return ChangeRecord(
                    id: id,
                    collection: collection,
                    type: type,
                    payload: payload,
                    hlcTimestamp: hlc,
                    authorPublicKey: authorPublicKey,
                    signature: signature
                )
            }
        }
    }

    public func applyChanges(_ changes: [ChangeRecord]) async throws {
        try await persistentContainer.performBackgroundTask { context in
            for change in changes {
                let key = "\(change.collection):\(change.id)"
                let request = NSFetchRequest<NSManagedObject>(entityName: "AirDbChangeEntity")
                request.predicate = NSPredicate(format: "compositeKey == %@", key)
                request.fetchLimit = 1

                let existing = try context.fetch(request).first
                if let existing = existing,
                   let existingHlc = existing.value(forKey: "hlcTimestamp") as? String,
                   HlcComparator.compare(change.hlcTimestamp, existingHlc) <= 0 {
                    continue
                }

                let target = existing ?? NSEntityDescription.insertNewObject(forEntityName: "AirDbChangeEntity", into: context)
                target.setValue(key, forKey: "compositeKey")
                target.setValue(change.collection, forKey: "collection")
                target.setValue(change.id, forKey: "recordId")
                target.setValue(Int16(change.type.rawValue), forKey: "mutationType")
                target.setValue(change.payload, forKey: "payload")
                target.setValue(change.hlcTimestamp, forKey: "hlcTimestamp")
                target.setValue(change.authorPublicKey, forKey: "authorPublicKey")
                target.setValue(change.signature, forKey: "signature")
                target.setValue(Date(), forKey: "createdAt")
            }

            if context.hasChanges {
                try context.save()
            }
        }
    }

    public func getLatestHlc() async throws -> String? {
        try await persistentContainer.performBackgroundTask { context in
            let request = NSFetchRequest<NSManagedObject>(entityName: "AirDbChangeEntity")
            request.sortDescriptors = [NSSortDescriptor(key: "hlcTimestamp", ascending: false)]
            request.fetchLimit = 1
            return try context.fetch(request).first?.value(forKey: "hlcTimestamp") as? String
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 2. Implementing AirDbAdapter
docs.text:
import AirDbKit
import Foundation
import GRDB

public final class GrdbAirDbAdapter: AirDbAdapter, @unchecked Sendable {
    private let dbWriter: any DatabaseWriter

    public init(dbWriter: any DatabaseWriter) {
        self.dbWriter = dbWriter
    }

    public func getChangesSince(sinceHlcTimestamp: String?, limit: Int) async throws -> [ChangeRecord] {
        try await dbWriter.read { db in
            let sql: String
            let arguments: StatementArguments

            if let since = sinceHlcTimestamp {
                sql = "SELECT * FROM _airdb_changes WHERE hlc_timestamp > ? ORDER BY hlc_timestamp ASC LIMIT ?"
                arguments = [since, limit]
            } else {
                sql = "SELECT * FROM _airdb_changes ORDER BY hlc_timestamp ASC LIMIT ?"
                arguments = [limit]
            }

            let rows = try Row.fetchAll(db, sql: sql, arguments: arguments)
            return rows.compactMap { row -> ChangeRecord? in
                guard let id: String = row["id"],
                      let collection: String = row["collection"],
                      let typeInt: Int = row["mutation_type"],
                      let type = MutationType(rawValue: typeInt),
                      let hlc: String = row["hlc_timestamp"] else {
                    return nil
                }

                return ChangeRecord(
                    id: id,
                    collection: collection,
                    type: type,
                    payload: row["payload"] ?? Data(),
                    hlcTimestamp: hlc,
                    authorPublicKey: row["author_public_key"],
                    signature: row["signature"]
                )
            }
        }
    }

    public func applyChanges(_ changes: [ChangeRecord]) async throws {
        try await dbWriter.write { db in
            for change in changes {
                // Apply LWW conflict resolution
                let existingHlc: String? = try String.fetchOne(
                    db,
                    sql: "SELECT hlc_timestamp FROM _airdb_changes WHERE collection = ? AND id = ?",
                    arguments: [change.collection, change.id]
                )

                if let existing = existingHlc, HlcComparator.compare(change.hlcTimestamp, existing) <= 0 {
                    continue
                }

                try db.execute(
                    sql: """
                    INSERT INTO _airdb_changes (collection, id, mutation_type, payload, hlc_timestamp, author_public_key, signature, created_at)
                    VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
                    ON CONFLICT(collection, id) DO UPDATE SET
                        mutation_type = excluded.mutation_type,
                        payload = excluded.payload,
                        hlc_timestamp = excluded.hlc_timestamp,
                        author_public_key = excluded.author_public_key,
                        signature = excluded.signature,
                        created_at = excluded.created_at
                    """,
                    arguments: [
                        change.collection,
                        change.id,
                        change.type.rawValue,
                        change.payload,
                        change.hlcTimestamp,
                        change.authorPublicKey,
                        change.signature,
                        Int64(Date().timeIntervalSince1970 * 1000)
                    ]
                )
            }
        }
    }

    public func getLatestHlc() async throws -> String? {
        try await dbWriter.read { db in
            try String.fetchOne(db, sql: "SELECT MAX(hlc_timestamp) FROM _airdb_changes")
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Apple Native SQLite Guide
docs.text: AirDbKit includes an out-of-the-box durable persistence engine: SqliteDbAdapter. It is implemented directly on top of Apple's system libsqlite3 C library, providing zero third-party dependencies.

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
• Zero External Dependencies: Relies strictly on Apple's built-in import SQLite3.
  • Write-Ahead Logging (WAL mode): Supports concurrent non-blocking reads while writing mutations.
  • Indexed HLC Range Queries: Fast delta queries using the idx_airdb_changes_hlc index.
  • Atomic Transactions: Batch changes are wrapped in immediate transactions (BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT).
  • Thread Safety: Fully thread-safe across Swift concurrency tasks using scoped locks.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
import AirDbKit
import Foundation

// 1. Locate documents directory for persistent storage
let documentsUrl = FileManager.default.urls(for: .documentDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
let databasePath = documentsUrl.appendingPathComponent("airdb_production.sqlite").path

// 2. Initialize the adapter
let adapter = try SqliteDbAdapter(databasePath: databasePath)

// 3. Initialize BLE Transport & Engine
let transport = CoreBluetoothTransport()
let engine = AirDbEngine(
    nodeName: "posko-field-ipad-01",
    adapter = adapter,
    transport = transport,
    clusterKey: clusterKey,
    authorKeyPair = authorKeyPair,
    enforceSignatures: true
)

await engine.start()

docs.title: 2. Implementing AirDbAdapter
docs.text:
import AirDbKit
import Foundation
import SwiftData

public final class SwiftDataAirDbAdapter: AirDbAdapter, @unchecked Sendable {
    private let container: ModelContainer

    public init(container: ModelContainer) {
        self.container = container
    }

    @MainActor
    public func getChangesSince(sinceHlcTimestamp: String?, limit: Int) async throws -> [ChangeRecord] {
        let context = container.mainContext

        var descriptor: FetchDescriptor<AirDbChangeEntity>
        if let since = sinceHlcTimestamp {
            descriptor = FetchDescriptor<AirDbChangeEntity>(
                predicate: #Predicate { $0.hlcTimestamp > since },
                sortBy: [SortDescriptor(\.hlcTimestamp, order: .forward)]
            )
        } else {
            descriptor = FetchDescriptor<AirDbChangeEntity>(
                sortBy: [SortDescriptor(\.hlcTimestamp, order: .forward)]
            )
        }
        descriptor.fetchLimit = limit

        let entities = try context.fetch(descriptor)
        return entities.compactMap { e in
            guard let type = MutationType(rawValue: e.mutationType) else { return nil }
            return ChangeRecord(
                id: e.recordId,
                collection: e.collection,
                type: type,
                payload: e.payload,
                hlcTimestamp: e.hlcTimestamp,
                authorPublicKey: e.authorPublicKey,
                signature: e.signature
            )
        }
    }

    @MainActor
    public func applyChanges(_ changes: [ChangeRecord]) async throws {
        let context = container.mainContext

        for change in changes {
            let key = "\(change.collection):\(change.id)"
            var fetchDesc = FetchDescriptor<AirDbChangeEntity>(predicate: #Predicate { $0.compositeKey == key })
            fetchDesc.fetchLimit = 1

            let existing = try context.fetch(fetchDesc).first
            if let existing = existing, HlcComparator.compare(change.hlcTimestamp, existing.hlcTimestamp) <= 0 {
                continue
            }

            if let existing = existing {
                existing.mutationType = change.type.rawValue
                existing.payload = change.payload
                existing.hlcTimestamp = change.hlcTimestamp
                existing.authorPublicKey = change.authorPublicKey
                existing.signature = change.signature
            } else {
                let entity = AirDbChangeEntity(
                    collection: change.collection,
                    recordId: change.id,
                    mutationType: change.type.rawValue,
                    payload: change.payload,
                    hlcTimestamp: change.hlcTimestamp,
                    authorPublicKey: change.authorPublicKey,
                    signature: change.signature
                )
                context.insert(entity)
            }
        }

        try context.save()
    }

    @MainActor
    public func getLatestHlc() async throws -> String? {
        let context = container.mainContext
        var desc = FetchDescriptor<AirDbChangeEntity>(
            sortBy: [SortDescriptor(\.hlcTimestamp, order: .reverse)]
        )
        desc.fetchLimit = 1
        return try context.fetch(desc).first?.hlcTimestamp
    }
}

docs.title: In-Memory KV Testing Adapter
docs.text: When developing automated test suites, running migrations or managing SQLite files on disk can slow down feedback loops. AirDB provides an in-memory key-value adapter (MemoryDbAdapter) designed for instant unit and integration testing.

docs.title: 1. Quick Usage
docs.text:
KotlinSwift 
import io.airdb.adapter.MemoryDbAdapter
import io.airdb.core.engine.AirDbEngine
import io.airdb.transport.sim.SimulatedTransport

val adapter = MemoryDbAdapter()
val transport = SimulatedTransport("test-node", simulatedNetwork)
val engine = AirDbEngine("test-node", adapter, transport)

engine.start()

import AirDbKit

// In AirDbKit, you can use the in-memory SQLite constructor for testing:
let adapter = try SqliteDbAdapter.inMemory()
let transport = SimulatedTransport(nodeId: 1, network: simulatedNetwork)
let engine = AirDbEngine(nodeName: "test-node", adapter: adapter, transport: transport)

await engine.start()

docs.title: 2. In-Memory Invariants
docs.text: The MemoryDbAdapter: - Stores records in concurrent, thread-safe hash maps (ConcurrentHashMap). - Implements the exact same Last-Write-Wins (LWW) conflict logic and tombstone tracking as disk-backed adapters. - Provides helper inspection methods like adapter.getAllRecords(collection) and adapter.clear() for fast test assertions.
